Most real networks are lumpy. Friends form circles, proteins form complexes, web pages cluster by
topic, and scientists collaborate within fields. A *community* is a group of nodes that are more
densely connected to one another than to the rest of the network, and *community detection* is
the task of finding such groups from the edges alone. EdgeCase provides more than a dozen
detection algorithms, along with tools for scoring a partition, comparing it with known groups,
and summarizing the result. This page covers all of them.

## A first example

Zachary's karate club is the standard first test for community detection, because the club really
did split in two, and the `faction` attribute records which side each member joined.
[`cmty_louvain()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_louvain.qmd) runs the Louvain algorithm, the most widely
used detection method, and stores each node's community in a `cmty_louvain` attribute:

::: {#ab511e57 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club().cmty_louvain()
karate.plot(color_by="cmty_louvain", label_by="label", seed=4)
```

## Detection algorithms

The algorithms take different approaches to the problem, and they differ in what they can handle
and how far they scale:

| Method | Approach | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [`cmty_louvain()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_louvain.qmd) | greedy modularity optimization with repeated aggregation | fast on very large graphs; uses edge weights |
| [`cmty_leiden()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_leiden.qmd) | Louvain with a refinement step that guarantees connected communities | fast, usually the best default; uses edge weights; optional CPM objective |
| [`cmty_fast_greedy()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_fast_greedy.qmd) | agglomerative modularity optimization (Clauset, Newman, and Moore) | fast |
| [`cmty_l_eigenvec()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_l_eigenvec.qmd) | repeated splitting by the leading eigenvector of the modularity matrix | graphs of up to a couple of thousand nodes |
| [`cmty_walktrap()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_walktrap.qmd) | merging nodes that short random walks connect | graphs of up to about a thousand nodes |
| [`cmty_edge_btwns()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_edge_btwns.qmd), [`cmty_girvan_newman()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_girvan_newman.qmd) | repeatedly removing the edge of highest betweenness | slow; graphs of a few hundred nodes |
| [`cmty_label_propagation()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_label_propagation.qmd), [`cmty_fast_label_propagation()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_fast_label_propagation.qmd), [`cmty_semisync_label_propagation()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_semisync_label_propagation.qmd) | nodes repeatedly adopting the community most common among their neighbors | very fast; accept directed graphs; results vary with `seed=` |
| [`cmty_fluid()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_fluid.qmd) | `k` communities that expand and compete like fluids | the number of communities is fixed |
| [`cmty_stochastic_block_model()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_stochastic_block_model.qmd) | fitting a stochastic block model by expectation-maximization | the number of blocks is fixed; finds any block structure, not only dense groups |
| [`cmty_k_clique()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_k_clique.qmd) | percolation of adjacent `k`-cliques | overlapping communities |

All of them except the label propagation methods and the stochastic block model require an
undirected graph. For a directed network, either use one of those, or convert the graph with
[`to_undirected()`](../reference/Graph.to_undirected.qmd), which returns an undirected copy and
leaves the original unchanged:

::: {#c96e7e06 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
votes = ec.wiki_vote().to_undirected().cmty_leiden(seed=1)
votes.get_node_df()["cmty_leiden"].n_unique()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4}
```
29
```
:::
:::


Leiden divides the 7,115 users of the Wikipedia election network into 29 communities in a
fraction of a second. Louvain and Leiden scale to graphs with millions of edges; at the other
extreme, the methods based on edge betweenness recompute every shortest path after each removal,
and are suited only to small graphs.

## Measuring the quality of a partition

A detection method always returns *some* partition, so it's important to be able to judge one.
The standard score is *modularity*, which compares the fraction of edges that fall inside
communities with the fraction expected if the edges were placed at random, keeping every node's
degree. [`modularity()`](../reference/Graph.modularity.qmd) computes it for any partition, given
as the name of a node attribute, as a dictionary of node IDs and communities, or as a list of node
groups:

::: {#5063f97b .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
round(karate.modularity("cmty_louvain"), 3), round(karate.modularity("faction"), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5}
```
(0.419, 0.371)
```
:::
:::


Values between 0.3 and 0.7 are typical of clear community structure, and putting every node in a
single community scores exactly 0. The Louvain partition scores higher than the real factions,
which is no surprise: Louvain is designed to maximize modularity, and the factions weren't. A
higher modularity means a partition fits the modularity criterion better, not that it is closer to
the truth.

[`partition_quality()`](../reference/Graph.partition_quality.qmd) returns two simpler scores.
*Coverage* is the fraction of edges inside communities, and *performance* is the fraction of node
pairs that the partition treats correctly: linked pairs in the same community, and unlinked pairs
in different ones.

::: {#21f356e2 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.partition_quality("cmty_louvain"), karate.partition_quality("faction")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6}
```
((0.7307692307692307, 0.803921568627451),
 (0.8717948717948718, 0.6167557932263814))
```
:::
:::


The two factions keep 87% of the friendships inside a group, against 73% for Louvain's four
communities, but they put many unlinked pairs together, so their performance is lower. Coverage
favors few, large communities and performance many small ones, so the two are best read together.

### Scoring single communities

[`conductance()`](../reference/Graph.conductance.qmd) scores one group of nodes: the number of
edges leaving the group, divided by the total degree of the group (or of the rest of the graph,
if that is smaller). A well-separated community has low conductance. Grouping the node table by
community gives the lists of members:

::: {#e0acf9ff .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
groups = (
    karate.get_node_df()
    .group_by("cmty_louvain")
    .agg("id")
    .sort("cmty_louvain")["id"]
    .to_list()
)
[round(karate.conductance(group), 3) for group in groups]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7}
```
[0.226, 0.25, 0.259, 0.417]
```
:::
:::


The last community, the six members on the administrator's periphery, is the least self-contained:
42% of its members' edges lead outside it. [`cut_size()`](../reference/Graph.cut_size.qmd),
[`normalized_cut_size()`](../reference/Graph.normalized_cut_size.qmd),
[`volume()`](../reference/Graph.volume.qmd), and
[`boundary_expansion()`](../reference/Graph.boundary_expansion.qmd) measure related quantities.

## Comparing with known groups

When the true groups are known, as with the karate club's factions or a benchmark graph, the
question is how well a method recovers them. EdgeCase doesn't provide a dedicated comparison
measure, but the most widely used one, the *adjusted Rand index* (ARI), is short to compute from
the node table. It counts the pairs of nodes on which two partitions agree, corrected for the
agreement expected by chance, so it is 1 for identical partitions and close to 0 for unrelated
ones:

::: {#4610eb49 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import math


def adjusted_rand(graph, a, b):
    df = graph.get_node_df()

    def pairs(columns):
        return sum(math.comb(count, 2) for count in df.group_by(columns).len()["len"])

    both, in_a, in_b = pairs([a, b]), pairs(a), pairs(b)
    expected = in_a * in_b / math.comb(df.height, 2)
    return (both - expected) / ((in_a + in_b) / 2 - expected)
```
:::

The methods that choose the number of communities themselves find three to five, and so agree
only partly with the two factions. [`cmty_fluid()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_fluid.qmd), told to find exactly
two communities, recovers the factions perfectly. This is a common pattern: when the number of
groups is known in advance, a method that takes it as an input often does better than one that
must also choose it.

### Randomness

Several methods use random choices, and accept `seed=` to make them reproducible. The label
propagation methods are the most sensitive to it, since a few early choices decide which labels
spread:

    round(adjusted_rand(karate.cmty_label_propagation(seed=seed), "faction", "cmty_label_propagation"), 2)

]

Across eight seeds, the agreement with the factions ranges from near zero to perfect. For any

## When structure is hard to detect

Community detection has limits, and a benchmark graph with planted communities shows them
clearly. [`add_planted_partition_graph()`](../reference/Graph.add_planted_partition_graph.qmd)
creates groups of nodes in which each pair within a group is linked with probability `p_in`, and
each pair in different groups with probability `p_out`, and records each node's true group in a
`community` attribute. Holding `p_out` fixed and lowering `p_in` makes the communities
progressively harder to see:

::: {#7572f884 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rows = []
for p_in in [0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.15, 0.12, 0.1]:
    planted = (
        ec.Graph()
        .add_planted_partition_graph(num_groups=4, group_size=50, p_in=p_in, p_out=0.05, seed=1)
        .cmty_leiden(seed=1)
    )
    rows.append(
        {
            "p_in": p_in,
            "found": planted.get_node_df()["cmty_leiden"].n_unique(),
            "ari": round(adjusted_rand(planted, "community", "cmty_leiden"), 3),
            "modularity_true": round(planted.modularity("community"), 3),
            "modularity_found": round(planted.modularity("cmty_leiden"), 3),
        }
    )
pl.DataFrame(rows)
```

While the groups are clearly denser inside than between, Leiden recovers them perfectly. Below
`p_in = 0.2` it fails abruptly: it finds more communities than were planted, and they bear little
relation to the true ones. Notice the last two columns. In the hard cases, the partition Leiden
finds has a *higher* modularity than the true one, because in any random graph some groups of
nodes happen to be a little denser than average, and modularity rewards them. Modularity values of
0.25 or so can arise from noise alone, so a modest score is not, on its own, evidence of real
community structure. [Graph generators](generators.qmd) describes
[`add_lfr_graph()`](../reference/Graph.add_lfr_graph.qmd), a more realistic benchmark with
skewed degrees and community sizes.

## Resolution

Modularity has a preferred scale. On large networks it tends to merge small communities that
should be separate, a weakness known as the *resolution limit*. Louvain, Leiden, and fast greedy
accept a `resolution=` argument that changes the scale: values above 1 favor more, smaller
communities, and values below 1 fewer, larger ones.

The Les Misérables character network, whose edges are weighted by the number of chapters in which
two characters appear together, shows the effect. Note that the modularity column scores every
partition at the standard resolution of 1, so that they can be compared:

::: {#5dba11bd .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
miserables = ec.les_miserables()
pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "resolution": resolution,
            "communities": len(set(partition.values())),
            "modularity": round(miserables.modularity(partition), 3),
        }
        for resolution in [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 4.0]
        for partition in [miserables.cmty_leiden(resolution=resolution, seed=1, return_dict=True)]
    ]
)
```

The number of communities rises steadily with the resolution, from three to 18, and the standard
modularity peaks at the default. There is no single correct resolution: a low one shows the
novel's main storylines, and a high one its individual scenes and households. Choose it to suit

`cmty_leiden(objective="cpm")` optimizes the *Constant Potts Model* instead of modularity (see
[`constant_potts_model()`](../reference/Graph.constant_potts_model.qmd)). Its resolution is a
density threshold: communities end up denser inside than the threshold and sparser between. CPM
has no resolution limit, so it can find small, dense groups in very large networks, but its
resolution must be set to suit each graph, with the graph's density a natural starting point.

### Hierarchies of communities

Louvain and Leiden work in levels, merging nodes into small communities, then merging those into
larger ones, and so on. [`cmty_louvain_levels()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_louvain_levels.qmd) and
[`cmty_leiden_levels()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_leiden_levels.qmd) return the partition at every
level, from finest to coarsest, as a list of dictionaries:

::: {#18061313 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
levels = miserables.cmty_louvain_levels()
[len(set(level.values())) for level in levels]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13}
```
[10, 5]
```
:::
:::


The first level groups the 77 characters into ten communities, and the second merges those into
six. Each level is a partition in its own right, and can be scored with `modularity()` or stored as
an attribute with [`set_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.set_node_attrs.qmd).

## A fixed number of groups

When the number of groups is known, or is part of the question, several methods take it as an
input:

| Method | Finds |
|---|---|
| [`cmty_fluid()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_fluid.qmd) | `k` communities of a connected graph |
| [`cmty_stochastic_block_model()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_stochastic_block_model.qmd) | `k` blocks of nodes with similar connection patterns |
| [`kernighan_lin_bisection()`](../reference/Graph.kernighan_lin_bisection.qmd) | two halves of equal size with few edges between them |
| [`spectral_modularity_bipartition()`](../reference/Graph.spectral_modularity_bipartition.qmd) | two groups, from the leading eigenvector of the modularity matrix |
| [`greedy_node_swap_bipartition()`](../reference/Graph.greedy_node_swap_bipartition.qmd) | two groups, by moving nodes one at a time to raise modularity |

The bisection methods return the two groups as a pair of sets of node IDs:

::: {#fe5ecad3 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
first, second = karate.spectral_modularity_bipartition()
sorted(first)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14}
```
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 17, 18, 20, 22]
```
:::
:::


The spectral split places 16 members with the instructor, and they are exactly the instructor's
faction.

The stochastic block model differs from the other methods in what it looks for. A block is a set
of nodes that connect to the rest of the network *in the same way*, which may mean being densely
linked to one another, but may also mean being linked to the same hub, or forming one side of a
bipartite structure. That makes it suited to finding core-periphery structure and roles, as well
as communities. The fit starts from a random assignment, so try several seeds. It stores its
blocks in a `sbm_block` attribute by default.

## Overlapping communities

The methods so far place every node in exactly one community, but in many networks a node belongs
to several: a person has a family, colleagues, and friends.
[`cmty_k_clique()`](../reference/Graph.cmty_k_clique.qmd) finds overlapping communities by
*clique percolation*. It builds every clique of `k` nodes, joins two cliques when they share
`k - 1` nodes, and reports the nodes of each joined group as a community. It returns the
communities as a list of lists of node IDs:

::: {#886232cc .cell execution_count=15}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karate.cmty_k_clique(k=4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15}
```
[[1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 14], [9, 31, 33, 34], [24, 30, 33, 34]]
```
:::
:::


With `k=4`, the club has three communities, and the administrator (ID 34) and member `"32"`
(ID 33) belong to two of them. Most members belong to none, since they aren't part of any
four-node clique. Smaller values of `k` give larger, looser communities.
[`overlapping_modularity()`](../reference/Graph.overlapping_modularity.qmd) scores an overlapping
cover in which every node belongs to at least one community.

## Local communities

Sometimes only one community matters: the one around a particular node. Rather than partition the
whole graph, [`greedy_source_expansion()`](../reference/Graph.greedy_source_expansion.qmd) grows a
community outward from a source node, adding the neighbor that best improves the community's
separation from the rest of the graph at each step, and returns its members as a set:

::: {#6d926cbe .cell execution_count=16}
``` {.python .cell-code}
sorted(karate.greedy_source_expansion(34))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16}
```
[3, 9, 10, 14, 15, 16, 19, 21, 23, 24, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 33, 34]
```
:::
:::


The community grown from the administrator contains 17 members: 15 of the 18 members of the
administrator's faction, and two of the instructor's, including their lieutenant (ID 3). A local method like this works on graphs too large to partition, since
it only examines the neighborhood of the source.

## Semi-supervised detection

When the communities of a few nodes are known, [`label_propagation()`](../reference/Graph.label_propagation.qmd)
spreads those labels to the rest of the graph: every unlabelled node repeatedly takes the label
most common among its neighbors, while the known labels stay fixed. Given only the two leaders,
it assigns the rest of the club:

::: {#47a86036 .cell execution_count=17}
``` {.python .cell-code}
predicted = karate.label_propagation({1: 0, 34: 1}, return_dict=True)
sum(predicted[node] != karate.get_node(node).attributes["faction"] - 1 for node in predicted)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17}
```
1
```
:::
:::


Only one of the 34 members ends up on the wrong side. Unlike the `cmty_*` methods, this is a
classification method: the labels come from you, and the graph only decides how far they spread.

## Working with the results

Since communities are stored as a node attribute, Polars does most of the work of summarizing
them. Here, Leiden divides the Les Misérables characters into six communities, and grouping by
community lists the best-connected characters of each:

::: {#d1afe221 .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code}
miserables = ec.les_miserables().cmty_leiden(seed=1)
(
    miserables.get_node_df()
    .group_by("cmty_leiden")
    .agg(
        size=pl.len(),
        main_characters=pl.col("label").sort_by("degree", descending=True).head(3),
    )
    .sort("cmty_leiden")
)
```

### A network of communities

[`quotient_graph()`](../reference/Graph.quotient_graph.qmd) collapses each community into a single
node, with an edge between two communities wherever any of their members are linked. It takes the
partition as a list of node groups, and records each new node's original members in a `members`
attribute:

groups = (
    miserables.get_node_df()
    .group_by("cmty_leiden")
    .agg("id")
    .sort("cmty_leiden")["id"]
    .to_list()
)
storylines = miserables.quotient_graph(groups)
storylines.get_node_df().select("label", "degree")

The quotient shows the main plot (block 1) at the center of the novel, linked to every other
storyline, while Myriel's household (block 0) connects only to it. For a closer look at one
community, [`subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.subgraph.qmd) extracts its members as a new graph, and
[Selections](selections.qmd) shows how to select a community with `select_nodes()` and act on
it.

Community structure feeds into many other analyses. [Similarity and link
prediction](similarity.qmd) covers link predictors that use communities, [Clustering and
motifs](clustering-and-motifs.qmd) the local density that communities are built from, and
[Network biology](network-biology.qmd) the testing of communities for enrichment in annotations.
